memoryText: But you, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Psalm 3:3 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
David wrote this verse while running from his own son. Everything he had was at risk, and yet he turned his eyes from the voices around him to the LORD.

“But you.” These two words are the hinge of the verse. Around David were enemies, rumors, and a suspicion that God had left him. But he sets one word against them all. When your circumstances say one thing, you may answer with “But you.”

“A shield about me.” A shield is held up between the warrior and the arrow. David says the LORD is not only in front of him but all around him. There is no side on which he is exposed.

“My glory.” David had lost his palace and his crown. If his honor depended on his position, he would have none. But his glory is God himself. No one can take that from him.

“The lifter of my head.” The ashamed hang their heads, and the defeated look at the ground. God lifts the chin of his people and lets them look him in the face.

The Christian reads this verse through Christ. He is our shield (Ephesians 6:16), he is the glory of God (John 1:14), and he lifts us out of shame (Romans 10:11). Say it today whenever you feel surrounded.
weekInReview: This week you read of Israel’s request for a king and the rise and first failure of Saul. You saw the ark in Philistia, where Dagon fell and the LORD showed that he needs no one’s help, and you read of the stone Ebenezer, “Till now the LORD has helped us.” You read Samuel’s warning about what kings take, and how Saul lost his kingdom at Gilgal because he feared the people more than he trusted God. In the Psalms you read the royal Psalm 2, where God answers rebellion by setting his King on Zion, and the prayers of David in Psalms 3 to 5 for morning and for evening. The week taught that God rules even when his people ask for the wrong thing, and that his anointed king is the only safe refuge.
reflectionQuestions: Saul acted out of fear when he should have waited on God. Where are you tempted to act in your own strength this week instead of waiting?
Psalm 2 says, “Blessed are all who take refuge in him.” How does Jesus, the Son and the anointed King, become a refuge for you in a specific worry?
Ebenezer means “Till now the LORD has helped us.” Write down three ways he has helped you in the last year.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he is a shield and the lifter of your head.
Thank him for the King he set on Zion.
Rest in the knowledge that he holds you.
